title: File errors, safe closing, buffering and portable text/binary modes (CodeSaathi extension)
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and its C rules.
Trace the example and identify data or resource flow.
Recognize relevant safety and failure cases.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: C streams may buffer output. Errors can occur during writes, flushes or close. fflush requests buffered output be delivered to the host environment; fclose closes the stream and can report delayed errors. Text and binary modes may differ on some systems.
understand.whyItMatters: Reliable file handling checks both the operation that writes data and the operation that finalizes the stream. Portable programs must choose text or binary mode intentionally.
understand.analogy: Treat each object or stream as a resource with a defined lifetime and explicit rules for access.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal object, storage-duration, alignment or library rules.

explain.narrative:
C streams may buffer output. Errors can occur during writes, flushes or close. fflush requests buffered output be delivered to the host environment; fclose closes the stream and can report delayed errors. Text and binary modes may differ on some systems.

Check all allocation, I/O and conversion results. Respect object bounds and lifetime, initialize data before reading it, and define who owns and releases each resource.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The program checks the append open, write, flush and close. A successful write call alone does not guarantee that later flushing and closing will succeed.

practise.guidedTask: Identify which calls may reveal a delayed output error.
practise.independentTask: Write a helper that appends a line to a file and reports failures without leaking an open stream.
hints: fclose invalidates the FILE pointer even if it reports an error; do not use the stream afterward.
Binary mode is important when the program needs byte-preserving file behaviour on systems that distinguish text and binary streams.
A successful close is not necessarily a guarantee of physical-media durability.
